---
title: Evaluating the Randomness of a Minigame Selection System

  html:

## 1 Introduction

Randomness is an essential component of many modern video games. From determining item
spawns to selecting maps and minigames, randomization majorly influences an individual’s
overall experience with a video game. Since random processes can produce streaks and
uneven outcomes, the human mind may interpret that as meaning certain outcomes appear
more than others; however, it can be difficult to determine whether these patterns are a
result of actual bias or simply chance. This is where statistics becomes essential, as
it provides objective methods for determining whether the observed patterns are from
bias or random variation.

One application of this question is in the video game *Hypixel Party Games*, where
players have speculated whether certain minigames were selected more than others. This
video game features 26 possible minigames, which 8 are selected per game session, each
theoretically having an equal chance of being selected. Using 10 independent samples
with around 325 games (2600 minigame selections) per sample, this analysis tests whether
the observed distribution is consistent with this expectation. If the game’s selection
was random, each minigame should appear at the expected frequency over a large amount of
games. The hypotheses are: 

* **Null hypothesis ($H_0$)**: The distribution of minigame selections follows the
expected uniform distribution under random selection. 
* **Alternate hypothesis ($H_1$)**: The distribution of minigame selections differs from
the expected uniform distribution under random selection.

## 2 Methodology

This study investigated whether the minigame selection in Hypixel Party Games produces
outcomes that are consistent with a uniform random distribution. Data were collected
across 10 independent trials. The sequence of minigames selected in each game was
extracted using optical character recognition (OCR); then, it was cleaned and compiled
into a structured dataset. The dataset was then analyzed in Python using a chi-square
goodness of fit test, corrected using a Monte Carlo simulation due to the
non-independent variables.

### 2.1 Data collection

Data were collected over multiple gameplay sessions and organized into 10 different
independent trials. To maximize the number of games collected within a feasible
timeframe, the data were collected by entering a game session, waiting for the game to
start, and then leaving without playing repeatedly for around 325 games. After all of
the games were collected, the replay feature on Hypixel was utilized in order to
determine the 8 minigames chosen in each individual game. This approach avoided the time
cost of completing all 8 minigames per game while still efficiently collecting the full
minigame sequence.

An automated data collection was programmed in order to reduce manual transcription and
improve accuracy. The program used OCR to extract the minigame names displayed on screen
during each replay. To ensure the accuracy of the OCR, extracted text was validated
against a reference list of each of the 26 possible minigame names; any output that did
not match an entry in this list was flagged as an OCR error and corrected manually.
Since the minigame names are very visually distinct from each other, the risk of one
minigame being misclassified as another is unlikely. Finally, for each minigame, the
trial number, game number, slot number, timestamp, and selected minigame were recorded
in a comma-separated values (CSV) file, allowing use for statistical analysis in Python.

Before analysis, the data from the CSV was imported into the pandas library from Python
in order to clean the data before statistical testing. The dataset was inspected for
missing, duplicate, and invalid records. Any incomplete or incorrectly recorded games
were removed before statistical testing. After removing 44 incomplete or incorrectly
recorded games, 3,318 games remained for statistical analysis, representing 26,544
individual minigame observations (3,318 games $\times$ 8 minigames per game).

### 2.2 Dataset structure

The collected data was organized into a CSV file containing the following columns:

| Column Name     | Description                                         |
| :-------------- | :-------------------------------------------------- |
| **trial**       | The trial in which the game was recorded.           |
| **game_number** | The sequential game number within each trial.       |
| **slot**        | The position of the minigame within the game (1-8). |
| **timestamp**   | The recorded start time of the game.                |
| **minigame**    | The name of the selected minigame.                  |

Each row represents one minigame observation. This format preserved the original data
while making it easier to summarize, filter, and analyze the data. 

### 2.3 Statistical analysis
The language Python was used along with the libraries numpy and pandas for the
statistical analysis. Analyses were performed at two different levels: separately for
each of the 10 individual trials, and for the combined dataset across all trials. This
allowed for an assessment of consistency across individual trials as well as an overall
test using the full combined sample.

Consistent with the hypotheses above, the null hypothesis states that each of the 26
minigames is equally likely to be chosen, meaning that $p_i = 1/26$ for $i = 1,...,26$,
while the alternate hypothesis states that at least one minigame has a selection
probability of $p_i \neq 1/26$. These hypotheses were evaluated separately for each
individual trial and for the combined dataset. A significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$
was used in all tests.

A chi-square goodness of fit was utilized in order to compare whether the observed
distribution significantly differs from $H_0$:

$$
\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{26} \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i}
$$

where $O_i$ represents the observed times minigame $i$ was selected, and $E_i$ is the
expected count under $H_0$. For a sample of $N$ games, the expected count for each
minigame in this experiment would be $E_i = N \times 8/26$.

The standard chi-square goodness of fit test assumes that each and every observation is
fully independent. However, this assumption does not apply to this experiment, as 8
minigames are chosen from 26 minigames without replacement. This introduces dependent
observations into the statistical test, reducing the variation within the distribution,
causing the value of the chi-square statistic ($\chi^2$) to decrease while inflating the
standard p value.

In order to account for this, a Monte Carlo simulation was performed to approximate the
value of $\chi^2$ performed under the null hypothesis. The simulation repeatedly
generated $N$ simulated games (100,000 iterations per test), where $N$ matched the
sample size of the trial or combined dataset being tested. Each simulated game consisted
of 8 minigames drawn without replacement from the 26 total options, mirroring the actual
selection process. A random seed value of 42 was used in numpy across all simulations to
ensure consistency and reproducibility. The corrected p value was then calculated by
comparing the amount of simulated $\chi^2$ values that were greater than or equal to the
actual observed chi-square value:

$$
p = \frac{(\text{number of simulated } X^2 \geq X^2_{obs}) + 1}{100,000 + 1}
$$

This corrected p value accounts for the dependence between minigame selections (a hypergeometric-type process) within a game, unlike the standard chi-square p value, which assumes independence.
